key_facts: The chapter covers: Connectivity (Paths and Circuits), Euler and Hamilton Paths, the Shortest Path Problem (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Ford's algorithm), and Graph Coloring.
A cut vertex (articulation point) is a vertex whose removal disconnects the graph; in Vietnamese: 'đỉnh cắt' hay 'điểm khớp'.
An Euler path is a path that traverses every edge of the graph exactly once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex exactly once.
Shortest path algorithms covered include Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm, and Floyd-Warshall algorithm.

The material is authored by Huynh Tuong Nguyen, Tran Tuan Anh, Nguyen An Khuong, and Le Hong Trang from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, University of Technology - VNUHCM, dated August 16, 2021.
A Hamilton circuit is defined as a circuit that visits each vertex in a graph exactly once.

Three rules of Hamilton Circuits are taught: (Rule 1) if deg(v) = 2, both edges incident to v must be used; (Rule 2) no subcircuit can be formed; (Rule 3) once two edges at a vertex v are determined, all other edges incident at v must be removed.
Property of Dijkstra's Algorithm: applicable for any graph G with any edge length ℓ(vi) ≥ 0, one-to-all shortest paths, time complexity O(|V|²).
Dijkstra's algorithm CAN be used on directed graphs (digraphs), but CANNOT be used on graphs with negative edge weights.

An application of Hamilton circuits is generating Gray Code: an n-digit Gray code can be generated by finding Hamilton circuits of an n-dimensional hypercube; Gray code is used in digital communication to reduce the effect of noise.
generated_text: Introduction to Graph Connectivity In the study of graphs, one of the most fundamental questions we can ask is whether the graph is 'whole' or composed of separate pieces. This lesson explores the concept of connectivity, which formalizes this idea for both undirected and directed graphs. Connectedness in Undirected Graphs Defining Connectivity An undirected graph is called connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices of the graph. This means that for any two vertices you pick in a connected graph, you can always find a way to get from one to the other by following the edges. A key consequence is that there is a simple path (a path that does not repeat vertices) between every pair of distinct vertices. If a graph is not connected, it is called disconnected . A disconnected graph is composed of two or more connected components , which are the separate, connected subgraphs within it. Measuring Connectivity: How Connected is a Graph? Some graphs are more robustly connected than others. We can measure this by identifying critical vertices and edges whose removal would disconnect the graph. A cut vertex (or articulation point) is a vertex that, if removed, would increase the number of connected components in the graph. A cut edge (or bridge) is an edge that, if removed, would increase the number of connected components. For example, in a graph where vertex 'b' is connected to 'a' on one side and to 'c' and 'g' on the other, removing 'b' would disconnect the graph. Therefore, 'b' is a cut vertex. Similarly, the edge '{a, b}' is a cut edge because removing it would isolate vertex 'a'. For graphs that are more densely connected, we can define connectivity more formally: A graph that has no cut vertices is called a nonseparable graph . A vertex cut is a set of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. The vertex connectivity , denoted κ(G), is the minimum number of vertices in a vertex cut. For example, if the smallest set of vertices that can disconnect a graph is {c, f}, then κ(G) = 2. An edge cut is a set of edges whose removal disconnects the graph. The edge connectivity , denoted λ(G), is the minimum number of edges in an edge cut. For example, if the smallest set of edges that can disconnect a graph is {{b, c}, {a, f}, {f, g}}, then λ(G) = 3. Connectedness in Directed Graphs For directed graphs, we must consider the direction of the edges. This leads to two different types of connectivity. Strongly Connected Graphs A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path from any vertex to any other vertex in the graph, following the direction of the edges. This means for any two vertices, 'a' and 'b', there is a path from 'a' to 'b' AND a path from 'b' to 'a'. Weakly Connected Graphs A directed graph is weakly connected if the underlying undirected graph is connected. This means that if we ignore the direction of all the edges, there is a path between any two vertices in the resulting undirected graph. Summary In this lesson, we defined graph connectivity. Key takeaways include: An undirected graph is connected if a path exists between any two vertices. Connectivity can be measured using cut vertices , cut edges , vertex connectivity (κ(G)) , and edge connectivity (λ(G)) . A directed graph is strongly connected if there is a path between any two vertices in both directions. A directed graph is weakly connected if its underlying undirected graph is connected.
